record.original_question: Decide whether every system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities is equivalent to a system in which all proportions are equal to 1; equivalently, determine whether every numerical semigroup that admits a Toms decomposition can be expressed as an intersection of modular numerical semigroups.

evidence.quote: Now we raise the following question: is every system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities equivalent to a system with all proportions being equal to one?, or equivalently, if a numerical semigroup admits a Tom decomposition, can it be expressed as an intersection of modular numerical semigroups?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of nonnegative integers. A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$.

Given positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $c \leq a$, the set
$$S(a,b,c) = \{ x \in \mathbb{N} : ax \bmod b \leq cx \}$$
is a numerical semigroup, called a proportionally modular numerical semigroup; the inequality $ax \bmod b \leq cx$ is called a proportionally modular Diophantine inequality, and the ratio $a/c$ is its proportion. When $c = 1$ the semigroup is simply called a modular numerical semigroup, and the inequality is called modular.

A system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities is a finite collection of such inequalities; its solution set is the intersection of the corresponding proportionally modular numerical semigroups. A numerical semigroup is said to admit a Toms decomposition if it is the solution set of some finite system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities, equivalently, if it can be written as a finite intersection of proportionally modular numerical semigroups.

Question: Is every system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities equivalent (i.e., has the same nonnegative integer solution set) to a system of inequalities all of which have proportion equal to $1$? Equivalently, can every numerical semigroup that admits a Toms decomposition be expressed as a finite intersection of modular numerical semigroups?
artifact.status_search_result: The question appears in a published numerical-semigroups problem list (2013) and is repeatedly referenced as an open question in subsequent literature on proportionally modular semigroups and Toms decompositions. Recent surveys and papers (through 2025) on irreducible decompositions of numerical semigroups still treat this reduction as an unresolved problem; no source found claiming a proof or counterexample.
